text: Google announced the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol in April 2025 to enable seamless communication and collaboration between AI agents, addressing interoperability issues within multi-agent systems. On June 23, 2025, Google donated this open standard to the Linux Foundation at the North American Open Source Summit to ensure neutral governance and industry-wide adoption. The donation was supported by over 100 technology companies including Amazon, Cisco, Microsoft, Salesforce, and others who contributed to the project's development. Under the Linux Foundation's management, A2A aims to promote community-driven innovation while mitigating vendor lock-in risks through its non-profit structure. Industry support has grown significantly since inception; as of April 9, 2026, more than 150 organizations are backing the protocol with active production deployments across supply chain, financial services, insurance, and IT operations sectors. Major cloud providers have integrated A2A into their platforms, such as Microsoft Azure AI Foundry and Copilot Studio alongside AWS Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The GitHub repository for A2A currently holds over 22,000 stars reflecting strong developer interest despite being less downloaded than competing protocols like MCP which saw approximately 24 times higher download volume in early comparisons. Security research published on August 28, 2025 identified critical vulnerabilities in the original specification including insufficient token lifetime control, lack of strong customer authentication, overly broad access scopes, and missing consent mechanisms that could lead to unauthorized data disclosure or privilege escalation. Researchers proposed protocol enhancements introducing explicit user consent orchestration and ephemeral scoped tokens to address these risks while maintaining low communication latency during empirical testing. The enhanced version released as draft v1.0 includes features such as signed agent cards for cryptographic identity verification and supports multiple interaction modes through request/response polling, server-sent events for streaming updates, and push notifications for long-running tasks. Agent discovery occurs via public metadata files known as Agent Cards published at well-known URIs which describe capabilities, skills, endpoints, and authentication requirements necessary for other agents to locate and interact with them securely.
